verses.text: Long ago, God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets many times and in many different ways.
But in these final days, he has spoken to us through his Son. God appointed him heir of everything, and through him he created the universe.

The Son is the shining brightness of God's glory and the exact expression of God's nature. He sustains everything by his powerful word. After he made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven.
So he became greater than the angels, just as the name he inherited is greater than theirs.
God never said to any angel, ‘You are my Son; today I have become your Father.’ And he never said, ‘I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.’
But when God brings his firstborn into the world, he says, ‘Let all God's angels worship him.’
About the angels, he says, ‘He makes his angels like winds, and his servants like flames of fire.’
But about the Son, he says, ‘Your throne, O God, lasts forever and ever. Your Kingdom's scepter is a scepter of justice.
You have loved what is right and hated what is wrong. That's why God, your God, has anointed you with joy beyond your companions.’
He also says, ‘Lord, in the beginning you laid the earth's foundation, and the heavens are the work of your hands.
They will wear out, but you remain. They will all grow old like clothing.
You will roll them up like a cloak, and they'll be changed. But you remain the same, and your years will never end.’
Has God ever said to an angel, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’?
All angels are serving spirits, sent to help those who will inherit salvation, aren't they?
So we must pay even closer attention to what we've heard, so we don't drift away.
If the message delivered through angels was reliable, and every violation or act of disobedience received a fair punishment,
how will we escape if we ignore such a great salvation? The Lord first announced it, and those who heard him confirmed it to us.
God also testified with them through signs, wonders, many kinds of miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit, distributed according to his will.
God did not place the world to come, which we're talking about, under the rule of angels.
Someone testified somewhere: ‘What are humans that you remember them, or human beings that you care for them?
You made them a little lower than the angels; you crowned them with glory and honor.
You placed everything under their feet.’ Since God placed everything under them, nothing was left outside their rule. But we don't yet see everything under their rule.
But we do see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for a short time. Because he suffered death, he is now crowned with glory and honor. By God's grace, he tasted death for everyone.
God, for whom and through whom everything exists, chose to bring many children to glory. So it was fitting that he make the pioneer of their salvation complete through suffering.
The one who makes people holy and those who are made holy all have one Father. That's why Jesus isn't ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.
He says, ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers and sisters; in the assembly I will sing your praise.’
Again he says, ‘I will trust him.’ And again, ‘Here I am with the children God has given me.’
Since the children share in flesh and blood, Jesus also shared in their humanity, so that through death he could destroy the one who held the power of death—the devil—
and free those who spent their whole lives trapped by fear of death.
Clearly, he doesn't help angels; he helps Abraham's descendants.
That's why he had to become like his brothers and sisters in every way, so he could be a merciful and faithful high priest in God's service and make atonement for the people's sins.
Since he suffered when he was tempted, he can help those who are being tempted.
So, holy brothers and sisters who share in the heavenly calling, focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest we confess.
He was faithful to the one who appointed him, just as Moses was faithful in all God's household.
Jesus deserves greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house deserves more honor than the house itself.
Every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything.
Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's household, and his service pointed to what would be said later.
But Christ is faithful as the Son over God's household. We are his household if we hold firmly to our courage and the hope we celebrate, right to the end.
So, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice,
don't harden your hearts as in the rebellion, during the testing in the wilderness,
where your ancestors tested me and put me to the test, even though they saw what I did for forty years.
That's why I was angry with that generation and said, ‘Their hearts are always wandering; they haven't understood my ways.’
So I swore in my anger, ‘They will never enter my rest.’
Brothers and sisters, be careful that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
Instead, encourage one another every day, while it's still called ‘today,’ so none of you will be hardened by sin's deception.
We share in Christ if we hold firmly to the confidence we had at the beginning, right to the end.
As Scripture says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, don't harden your hearts as in the rebellion.’
Who were the ones who heard and rebelled? Weren't they all the people Moses led out of Egypt?
Who was God angry with for forty years? Wasn't it those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?
And to whom did God swear they would never enter his rest? Wasn't it those who disobeyed?
So we see that they couldn't enter because they didn't believe.
So be careful, or one of you may miss the promise of entering God's rest.
We've heard the Good News just as they did. But their message did them no good, because they didn't join what they heard with faith.
But we who have believed do enter that rest. God said, ‘In my anger I swore they would never enter my rest,’ even though his works were finished since the creation of the world.
Somewhere God spoke about the seventh day: ‘God rested on the seventh day from all his work.’
And in this passage he says again, ‘They will never enter my rest.’
Since it remains true that some will enter that rest, and those who first heard the Good News failed to enter because of disobedience,
God set another day—‘Today’—when, long afterward, he spoke through David, as already quoted: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, don't harden your hearts.’
If Joshua had given them rest, God wouldn't have spoken later about another day.
So a Sabbath rest remains for God's people.
Those who enter God's rest also rest from their work, just as God rested from his.
So let's make every effort to enter that rest, so no one will fall by following the same example of disobedience.
God's word is alive and active, sharper than any double-edged sword. It cuts through to divide soul and spirit, joints and marrow, and judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Nothing in creation is hidden from God. Everything is exposed and laid bare before the eyes of the one to whom we must give an account.
So since we have a great high priest who has gone through the heavens—Jesus, the Son of God—let's hold firmly to what we believe.
We don't have a high priest who can't understand our weaknesses. He was tempted in every way just as we are, but he didn't sin.
So let's approach the throne of grace with confidence, where we'll receive mercy and find grace to help us when we need it.
Every high priest is chosen from among people and appointed to represent them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins.
A high priest can deal gently with those who don't understand and those who have gone astray, because he too is subject to weakness.
Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as for the people's sins.
No one takes this honor for themselves. They must be called by God, just as Aaron was.
In the same way, Christ didn't take the honor of becoming high priest for himself. God said to him, ‘You are my Son; today I have become your Father.’
And elsewhere God says, ‘You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.’
During his life on earth, Jesus prayed and pleaded with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death. Because of his reverent submission, God heard him.
Although he was the Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.
After being made complete, he became the source of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys him,
and God appointed him high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
We have much to say about this, but it's hard to explain because you've become slow to understand.
By now you should be teachers, but you still need someone to teach you the basic truths of God's message. You need milk, not solid food.
Anyone who lives on milk is inexperienced in the message about righteousness, like a baby.
Solid food is for mature people, who have trained themselves through practice to distinguish good from evil.
So let's move beyond the basic teaching about Christ and grow toward maturity. We don't need to lay the foundation all over again: turning from dead works, faith in God,
teaching about baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.
And we'll do this, if God allows.
Some people have once been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit,
and tasted the goodness of God's word and the powers of the age to come,
but then fallen away. It's impossible to renew them to repentance again, since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again and exposing him to public disgrace.
Land that soaks up frequent rain and produces a crop useful to those who farm it receives God's blessing.
But land that grows thorns and weeds is worthless and close to being cursed; in the end it will be burned.
Even though we're speaking this way, dear friends, we're convinced better things are true of you—things that belong with salvation.
God isn't unjust. He won't forget your work and the love you've shown for his name by serving his people, as you still do.
We want each of you to show the same dedication, so your hope will be fully realized to the end.
Don't become lazy. Instead, imitate those who inherit God's promises through faith and patience.
When God made his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater to swear by.
He said, ‘I will surely bless you and make your descendants very numerous.’
After patiently waiting, Abraham received what God had promised.
People swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath settles a dispute as a final confirmation.
God wanted to make the unchanging nature of his purpose especially clear to those who would inherit the promise, so he guaranteed it with an oath.
God did this so that, through two unchangeable things—in which it's impossible for God to lie—we who have fled to him for refuge would be strongly encouraged to hold on to the hope set before us.
We have this hope as a sure and steady anchor for our souls. It reaches behind the curtain into the inner sanctuary,
where Jesus has gone ahead of us as our forerunner. He became a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham on his way back from defeating the kings and blessed him.
Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means ‘king of righteousness,’ and he was also king of Salem, meaning ‘king of peace.’
He has no recorded father or mother or family line, no beginning of life or end of days. Like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.
Think about how great he was: even Abraham the patriarch gave him a tenth of the best part of the plunder.
The descendants of Levi who become priests are commanded by the law to collect a tenth from the people—their own relatives, even though they too are descended from Abraham.
But Melchizedek, who wasn't descended from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed the one who had received God's promises.
No one disputes that the greater person blesses the lesser.
In one case, people who die collect a tenth; in the other, Scripture testifies that the one who received it lives on.
We could even say that Levi, who collects tithes, paid a tithe through Abraham,
because Levi was still in his ancestor's body when Melchizedek met Abraham.
If the Levitical priesthood could bring perfection (and under it the people received the law), why was another priest needed, one in the order of Melchizedek instead of Aaron?
When the priesthood changes, the law must change too.
The one these things are said about belonged to a different tribe, and no one from that tribe ever served at the altar.
It's clear that our Lord came from Judah, a tribe Moses never connected with priesthood.
This becomes even clearer when another priest like Melchizedek appears,
one who became a priest not through a law about physical ancestry, but through the power of an indestructible life.
Scripture testifies, ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
The earlier command is set aside because it was weak and ineffective
(the law made nothing perfect). A better hope has now been introduced, and through it we draw near to God.
Jesus didn't become a priest without an oath.

The others became priests without an oath, but Jesus became a priest with an oath from the one who said, ‘The Lord has sworn and won't change his mind: You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.
There have been many priests, because death kept them from continuing in office.
But Jesus lives forever, so his priesthood never passes to anyone else.
That's why he can save completely those who come to God through him. He always lives to speak to God on their behalf.
We need just this kind of high priest: holy, innocent, pure, set apart from sinners, and raised above the heavens.
He doesn't need to offer sacrifices every day like other high priests—first for his own sins and then for the people's. He did this once for all when he offered himself.
The law appoints weak men as high priests, but the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, who has been made perfect forever.
Here's the main point of what we're saying: we have a high priest like this, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven.
He serves in the holy place, the true tent set up by the Lord, not by a human being.
Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. So this high priest also had to have something to offer.
If he were on earth, he wouldn't be a priest at all, since there are already priests who offer gifts according to the law.

They serve in a place that is only a copy and shadow of what's in heaven. Moses was warned by God before he built the tent: ‘Be sure to make everything according to the pattern you were shown on the mountain.’
But Jesus has received a ministry far greater than theirs, just as the covenant he mediates is better and rests on better promises.
If the first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no need to look for a second.
But God found fault with the people and said: ‘The days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah.

It won't be like the covenant I made with their ancestors when I took them by the hand and led them out of Egypt. They didn't remain faithful to my covenant, so I turned away from them, says the Lord.

This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people.
No longer will each person teach a neighbor or a brother and say, ‘Know the Lord.’ Everyone, from the least to the greatest, will know me.
I will forgive their wrongdoing and never again remember their sins.’
By calling it a new covenant, God has made the first one outdated. And what is outdated and growing old will soon disappear.
The first covenant had rules for worship and an earthly sanctuary.
A tent was set up. In its first room were the lampstand, the table, and the bread set before God. This room was called the Holy Place.
Behind the second curtain was the room called the Most Holy Place.
It contained the gold incense altar and the covenant chest, covered with gold. Inside were a gold jar of manna, Aaron's staff that had budded, and the covenant tablets.
Above the chest were the glorious cherubim overshadowing the place of atonement. We can't discuss these things in detail now.
With everything arranged this way, the priests regularly entered the first room to carry out their service.
But only the high priest entered the second room, and only once a year, bringing blood to offer for himself and for the people's sins committed in ignorance.
By this, the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place wasn't yet open as long as the first tent was still standing.
This is an illustration for the present time. Gifts and sacrifices are offered, but they can't make the worshiper's conscience clear.
They deal only with food and drink and various ritual washings—outward rules that last until the time of renewal.
But when Christ came as high priest of the good things now here, he went through the greater and more perfect tent, not made by human hands and not part of this creation.
He didn't enter by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, entering the Most Holy Place once for all and securing eternal redemption.
If the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean can make their bodies clean,
how much more will Christ's blood cleanse our consciences from useless deeds so we can serve the living God? Through the eternal Spirit, Christ offered himself to God without blemish.

That's why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant. A death has taken place to set people free from the sins committed under the first covenant, so those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.
Where there is a will, the death of the one who made it must be established.
A will takes effect only after someone has died; it has no force while the person who made it is still alive.
That's why even the first covenant wasn't put into effect without blood.
After Moses had announced every commandment to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people.
He said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant God commanded you to keep.’
In the same way, he sprinkled the tent and all the objects used in worship with blood.
According to the law, almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without blood being shed there is no forgiveness.
So the copies of the heavenly things had to be cleansed with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves required better sacrifices.
Christ didn't enter a holy place made by human hands, which is only a copy of the true one. He entered heaven itself, and now appears in God's presence for us.
He didn't enter heaven to offer himself over and over, the way the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that isn't his own.
Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer again and again since the world began. Instead, he has appeared once at the culmination of the ages to remove sin by offering himself.
People are appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment.
In the same way, Christ was offered once to carry the sins of many. He will appear a second time—not to deal with sin, but to save those who are waiting eagerly for him.
The law is only a shadow of the good things coming, not the things themselves. So the same sacrifices, offered year after year, can never make those who come near perfect.
If they could, wouldn’t the sacrifices have stopped? The worshipers would have been cleansed once for all and would no longer feel guilty about their sins.
Instead, those sacrifices remind people of their sins every year.
It’s impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take sins away.
That’s why, when Christ came into the world, he said: “You didn’t want sacrifices and offerings, but you prepared a body for me.
You weren’t pleased with burnt offerings or sin offerings.
Then I said, ‘Look, I have come to do your will, God; it’s written about me in the scroll.’”
First he says, “You didn’t want sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings, and you weren’t pleased with them”—even though the law required them.
Then he says, “Look, I have come to do your will.” He removes the first arrangement to establish the second.
By that will, we have been made holy through the offering of Jesus Christ’s body, once for all.
Every priest stands day after day doing his service and offering the same sacrifices again and again. Those sacrifices can never take sins away.
But after Christ offered one sacrifice for sins forever, he sat down at God’s right hand.
Since then, he’s waiting until his enemies are put under his feet.
By one offering he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy.
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First he says:
“This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them on their minds.”
Then he adds: “I will no longer remember their sins and lawless acts.”
When these are forgiven, there’s no longer any need for an offering for sin.
So, brothers and sisters, we can enter the Most Holy Place with confidence because of Jesus’ blood.
He opened a new and living way for us through the curtain—that is, through his body.
And we have a great priest over God’s household.
So let’s come near with a sincere heart and complete confidence in faith. Our hearts have been cleansed from a guilty conscience, and our bodies have been washed with pure water.
Let’s hold tightly to the hope we confess without wavering, because the one who made the promise is faithful.
Let’s think about how to spur one another on to love and good deeds.
Let’s not stop meeting together, as some have made a habit of doing. Instead, let’s encourage one another, especially as you see the Day coming closer.
If we deliberately keep sinning after learning the truth, there’s no sacrifice for sins left.
There’s only a terrifying expectation of judgment and a raging fire ready to consume God’s enemies.
Anyone who rejected Moses’ law died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.
How much worse punishment do you think someone deserves who tramples God’s Son, treats the covenant blood that made them holy as something ordinary, and insults the Spirit of grace?
We know the one who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge his people.”
It’s terrifying to fall into the hands of the living God.
Remember those earlier days. After you received the light, you endured a hard struggle with suffering.
Sometimes you were publicly shamed and mistreated; other times you stood alongside people who were treated that way.
You showed compassion to me while I was in prison, and you gladly accepted the loss of your possessions, knowing you had something better and lasting in heaven.
So don’t throw away your confidence; it brings a great reward.
You need endurance, so that after doing God’s will, you’ll receive what he promised.
“In just a little while, the one who is coming will come and won’t delay.
But my righteous one will live by faith. If he pulls back, I take no pleasure in him.”
We aren’t among those who pull back and are destroyed. We are among those who trust God and are saved.
Faith means being sure of what we hope for and convinced about what we can’t see.
It was by faith that people long ago were commended.
By faith we understand that the universe was formed by God’s word, so what is visible came from what can’t be seen.

By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. Because of that faith he was commended as righteous, with God himself testifying about his gifts. Abel still speaks through his faith, even though he died.
By faith Enoch was taken away so he wouldn’t see death. He couldn’t be found because God had taken him. Before he was taken, he was commended as someone who pleased God.
Without faith it’s impossible to please God, because whoever comes to him must believe that he exists and rewards those who seek him.
By faith Noah, warned about things not yet seen, honored God and built an ark to save his family. His faith condemned the world, and he received the righteousness that comes through faith.
By faith Abraham obeyed when God called him to leave for a place he would later receive as his inheritance. He left without knowing where he was going.
By faith he lived as a foreigner in the promised land, like a stranger in a country that wasn’t his. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who shared the same promise.
He was looking forward to the city with lasting foundations, whose architect and builder is God.
By faith Sarah received strength to conceive, even though she was past the age, because she considered the one who promised faithful.
So from one man, who was as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and the countless grains of sand on the seashore.
All these people died in faith without receiving what was promised. They saw it from far away, welcomed it, and admitted they were foreigners and strangers on earth.
People who talk like that show they’re looking for a homeland.
If they had been thinking about the place they left, they could have gone back.
Instead, they were longing for a better homeland—a heavenly one. So God isn’t ashamed to be called their God, because he prepared a city for them.
By faith Abraham, when tested, offered Isaac. He was ready to offer his only son, even though he had received the promises,
and God had told him, “Your descendants will come through Isaac.”
Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead, and in a sense he received Isaac back from death.
By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning what was to come.
By faith Jacob, as he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped while leaning on his staff.
By faith Joseph, near the end of his life, spoke about Israel’s departure and gave instructions about his bones.
By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after he was born, because they saw he was a beautiful child and weren’t afraid of the king’s order.
By faith Moses, when he grew up, refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.
He chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy sin’s fleeting pleasures.
He considered disgrace for the Messiah greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures, because he was looking ahead to his reward.
By faith he left Egypt without fearing the king’s anger. He kept going because he saw the one who is invisible.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so the destroyer of the firstborn wouldn’t touch Israel’s children.
By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as if on dry ground, but when the Egyptians tried, they drowned.
By faith Jericho’s walls fell after the people marched around them for seven days.
By faith Rahab the sex worker welcomed the spies in peace and didn’t die with those who disobeyed.
What more can I say? I don’t have time to tell about Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets.
Through faith they conquered kingdoms, did what was right, received what was promised, shut the mouths of lions,
put out raging fires, escaped the sword, were made strong after being weak, became powerful in battle, and drove back foreign armies.
Women received their dead back to life. Others were tortured and refused release, wanting a better resurrection.
Some faced mocking and whipping, and even chains and prison.
They were stoned; they were sawed in two; they were killed by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, persecuted, and mistreated.
The world wasn’t worthy of them. They wandered through deserts and mountains, living in caves and holes in the ground.
All these people were commended for their faith, but they didn’t receive what was promised,
because God had planned something better for us, so that only together with us would they be made complete.

So then, since we’re surrounded by such a huge crowd of witnesses, let’s throw off everything that weighs us down, especially the sin that so easily traps us. Let’s run with endurance the race set before us,
keeping our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith. For the joy ahead of him, he endured the cross, ignoring its shame, and sat down at the right hand of God’s throne.
Think carefully about him, who endured such hostility from sinners, so you don’t grow tired and give up.
In your struggle against sin, you haven’t yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
And you’ve forgotten the encouragement that speaks to you like children: “My child, don’t take the Lord’s discipline lightly, and don’t give up when he corrects you.
For the Lord disciplines the one he loves and corrects every child he welcomes.”
Endure hardship as discipline: God is treating you as his children. What child isn’t disciplined by a parent?
If you aren’t disciplined—which everyone receives—then you aren’t legitimate children; you aren’t really part of the family.
We had human parents who disciplined us, and we respected them. Shouldn’t we submit even more to the Father of spirits and live?
Our parents disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so we can share in his holiness.
No discipline feels good at the time; it’s painful. But later it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness in those trained by it.
So strengthen your tired hands and weak knees.
Make straight paths for your feet, so what is weak won’t be injured but will be healed.
Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy. Without holiness no one will see the Lord.
Make sure no one misses God’s grace, and don’t let a bitter root grow up and cause trouble, poisoning many.
Make sure no one is sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who traded his birthright for one meal.
You know that afterward, when he wanted the blessing, he was rejected. He found no chance to change his father’s mind, even though he begged with tears.
You haven’t come to a mountain you can touch, blazing with fire, darkness, gloom, and storm.
You haven’t heard a trumpet blast and a voice speaking words that made the hearers beg for no more.
They couldn’t bear the command: “Even if an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.”
The sight was so terrifying that Moses said, “I’m trembling with fear.”
Instead, you’ve come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem, and countless angels celebrating together.
You’ve come to the gathering of God’s firstborn, whose names are written in heaven. You’ve come to God, the judge of everyone, and to the spirits of righteous people made complete.
You’ve come to Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, and to sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s.
Be careful not to refuse the one who speaks. If those who rejected the warning on earth didn’t escape, how much less will we escape if we turn away from the one who warns us from heaven?
Back then his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised: “Once more I’ll shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
The words “once more” show that what can be shaken will be removed—created things—so that what can’t be shaken will remain.
So, since we’re receiving a kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s be thankful and worship God acceptably, with reverence and awe,
because our God is a consuming fire.
Keep showing family love to one another.
Don’t forget to welcome strangers, because some people have welcomed angels without knowing it.
Remember those in prison as if you were imprisoned with them. Remember those who are mistreated, since you’re also in a body that can suffer.
Let marriage be honored by everyone, and let the marriage bed stay pure, because God will judge sexually immoral people and adulterers.
Keep your life free from the love of money, and be content with what you have, because God has said: “I will never leave you; I will never abandon you.”
So we can confidently say: “The Lord is my helper; I won’t be afraid. What can anyone do to me?”
Remember your leaders, who spoke God’s word to you. Look at the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
Don’t get swept away by all kinds of strange teachings. It’s good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by food rules that never helped those who followed them.
We have an altar, and those who serve at the tent have no right to eat from it.
The bodies of animals whose blood the high priest brings into the sanctuary as a sin offering are burned outside the camp.
That’s why Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to make the people holy through his own blood.
So let’s go to him outside the camp, carrying the shame he carried.
Here we don’t have a lasting city; we’re looking for the city that’s coming.
So let’s continually offer God a sacrifice of praise through Jesus—the fruit of lips that openly acknowledge his name.
And don’t forget to do good and share what you have, because God is pleased with sacrifices like these.
Obey your leaders and cooperate with them, because they keep watch over your souls and will give an account. Let them do this with joy, not groaning, because that wouldn’t help you.
Pray for us. We’re sure we have a clear conscience and want to live honorably in every way.
I especially urge you to pray so I can be restored to you soon.
May the God of peace, who brought our Lord Jesus back from the dead—the great Shepherd of the sheep—by the blood of an everlasting covenant,
equip you with everything good to do his will. May he work in us what pleases him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, please bear with this word of encouragement. I’ve written to you briefly.
I want you to know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he comes soon, I’ll visit you with him.
Greet all your leaders and all God’s people. The believers from Italy send you greetings.
Grace be with you all. Amen.
